A closer look at the interaction of motivational focus by distance
showed that when participants focus on showing their support
(signaling), distance has no effect on the probability of making a
donation (nearby: 55.37% vs. far away: 60.13%; Wald  .94, p 
.33). However, when their motivational focus is on helping others
(impact), the probability is greater that participants will donate
when Haiti is described as nearby (62.14%) than when it is
described as far away (44.56%; Wald  4.28, p  .039; see Figure
3). These results support the notion that people are more likely to
engage in social actions for nearby (vs. faraway) causes because
they expect to make a greater impact.

Are Interest Rates Higher?—In this section, I test whether borrowers in inflated 
transactions are more likely to pay higher mortgage rates. The sample used consists 
of 57,788 mortgages in which lenders voluntarily report annualized percentage rates 
(APRs) post-2003.28
The tests of the relation between seller hints, foreclosure, and mortgage prices is 
presented in Table 5, columns 3, 6, and 7. Column 3 repeats the foreclosure likeli-
hood tests (from columns 1 and 2) for the sample that is used to study interest rates. 
The results show that the likelihood of foreclosure for highly leveraged borrow-
ers is statistically weak (t = 0.8 to 1.2) due to the small sample size; however, the 
coefficients are large and economically significant (the likelihood of foreclosure is 
higher by 1.3 percent (9.2 percent) for those who, with an LTV of 95–100 percent 
(> 100 percent), buy properties that include sellers’ hints relative to those who do 
not). Columns 6 and 7 show that borrowers with LTV of 95–100 percent who buy 
properties with sellers’ hints pay interest rates that are higher by 0.05–0.27 percent; 
further, these rates are not monotonic and therefore do not seem to reflect the risk 
that increases with leverage.

Procedure
The study proceeded in seven phases.
Phase 1: Baseline affect.  First, participants rated how 
happy they felt “right now” using the Valence subscale of 
the Self-Assessment Manikin (Bradley & Lang, 1995). Par-
ticipants responded to the item using a scale from 1 (very 
unhappy) to 9 (very happy; M = 6.36, SD = 1.34).
Phase 2: Baseline EEG.  Next, participants were told 
that their brain activity would be noninvasively moni-
tored using EEG. After the attachment of the electrodes, 
baseline EEG was recorded during both an eyes-open 
and an eyes-closed resting period for 3 min each, with 
the order of the two counterbalanced across participants 
(see Physiological Recording and Processing section for 
more details on EEG recording).

baseline EEG recording was obtained, participants com-
